tagline: Forests, farms and mill towns along the Pend Oreille
intro: The Panhandle Historic Rivers Passage follows US 2 along the north shore of the Pend Oreille River, from the Washington line to Sandpoint. Visit Idaho presents this scenic byway as a drive past forests and farms, with opportunities to learn how the Ice Age and Great Missoula Floods shaped northern Idaho. Its published distance is 29.9 miles and its driving time is 40 minutes. The route forms the southern leg of the International Selkirk Loop. The tourism office’s 2013 description records a two-lane road without passing lanes, with river scenery framed by forests and farms.

Riverboats and railroads served the settlements before automobile travel made better roads and a river bridge priorities near Newport. Newspaper editor Fred L. Wolf campaigned for that bridge. Governor Ernest Lister vetoed a proposal in 1913, but a crossing finally opened on June 15, 1927, improving travel between northeastern Washington and northern Idaho. The original bridge was replaced in 1989.

Begin at Oldtown, then pass Albeni Falls Dam on the way to Priest River. Laclede stands where Riley Creek meets the Pend Oreille beside US 2. Continue through Dover to Sandpoint, where the journey reaches Lake Pend Oreille and a town whose economy was built on timber and railroads.

moments.title: Oldtown
moments.text: Oldtown and Newport share a built-up area divided by a straight state boundary, with no natural barrier between them. The Idaho settlement was once called Newport, Idaho, and served as a port and supply point for the Pend Oreille Valley. As settlement expanded on the Washington side, the post office moved there and the Idaho settlement declined. It incorporated as Oldtown in April 1947. The river and state line leave its main business district along US 2 just 700 feet of space on the Idaho side. Rail connections and the river carried timber and other goods from the surrounding region.

moments.title: Albeni Falls Dam
moments.text: Albeni Falls Dam occupies the site of a natural waterfall on the Pend Oreille River between Oldtown and Priest River. The falls were named for Albeni Poirier, a French immigrant who settled here in 1887. The Army Corps of Engineers began construction in 1951 to control flooding and supply electricity to the growing Pacific Northwest. Completed in 1955, the dam is 90 feet high and 775 feet long, including a 400-foot spillway. The Corps operates the dam, whose electricity goes to the Bonneville Power Administration, adding power generation to this former waterfall site.

moments.title: Dover
moments.text: More than 50 buildings traveled upriver on barges when A.C. White moved its mill town from Laclede to Dover. The company bought Dover Lumber Company in 1922 after its Laclede mill burned, then moved the buildings with horses and winches. One relocated building became Dover Church. Designed as a summer cottage for the White family, it was unfinished when the mill burned. Whitehouse & Price designed the cottage, which was built in 1922; its barge journey followed in 1923, after the fire. Its eventual use as a church gave a rustic domestic design a different purpose.
